title: Where the Data Lives: Multi-Region Operation and Data Residency

know: The difference between data residency (where data is stored) and data localization (a law that requires it), and what active-active and active-passive mean.
The Reserve Bank of India's 2018 storage rule and its 2019 clarification, and what Stripe's India page (updated 2023) says the move cost in features.

What is documented about hosting: Stripe on Amazon Web Services (2023, 2024, current documentation); Adyen on its own infrastructure in data centers (2021, 2025, 2026) with five integration regions named and its data centers listed by continent or country.

What is not public for either company: which AWS regions Stripe uses and how many, the cities of Adyen's data centers, and how one region or data center takes over from another (Adyen states only that its load balancers fail over between data centers).
believe: A localization law is a product constraint as much as a storage one: identifiers, saved cards and fraud signals stop crossing the border.
A statement about a provider's regions or failover that the provider has not published should be asked for in writing, not inferred.
can_do: Answer 'where is our customers' payment data' for each provider with what is documented, and list what must be asked of the provider.
Say what a new localization rule would change for stored cards, fraud checks and reporting in the affected country.

audience.who: A software engineer or architect who has read the chapters on reliability and on data stores and is asked, by a customer, an auditor or a colleague, where a payment provider keeps data and what happens when a region fails.
already_knows: Regions, replication and failover as general engineering.
Shards and the consistency boundary (payment-data-stores-and-consistency) and the unknown outcome (payment-reliability-and-availability).
Larkfield, its two providers and the studios that use both (meet-larkfield).
does_not_know: Data residency against data localization; the Reserve Bank of India's storage rule.
What Stripe and Adyen have each published about hosting, regions and India, and what neither has published.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a confident sentence about a provider's regions, the reader separates the part the public record supports from the parts it does not.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A colleague writes in a design document: 'Stripe runs active-active in three AWS regions, so our European members' data never leaves the EU.' Which parts of this sentence does the public record support, as of November 2026?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Only that Stripe runs on AWS. No AWS region is named and no count given; Stripe states active-active nowhere; Stripe's data-processing documents describe transfer mechanisms for European personal data, and no EU-residency product statement was found. The sentence should be replaced by a question to the provider.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a new localization law in a country the chapter does not discuss, the reader names what changes for a merchant, going by the documented India case.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A country announces that payment data about transactions in the country must be stored only inside it. Going by what happened in India, name three things a merchant using a global provider there should expect to change.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Any three of: data for that country is stored on servers in the country and kept apart; saved payment details cannot be copied in or out; the same card gets a different fingerprint there than elsewhere, so duplicate and fraud checks stop matching across the border; some features (Stripe listed its card updater, revenue recognition in Billing and its Sigma reporting product) are disabled or changed; processing abroad may still be allowed with a deadline to bring the data back (24 hours in India's 2019 clarification).

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter contains no inferred topology: every Stripe and Adyen statement about hosting, regions or failover is a dated documented fact or the words 'not public', and a named section lists where the evidence stops.
The chapter is no longer than its evidence: it does not exceed about 3,800 words before Sources and Evidence.

thesis.question: What decides where a payment platform runs and where its data stays, and how much of Stripe's and Adyen's answer is public?
thesis.claim: Where a localization law applies, it settles where payment data is stored before any latency or availability goal, and elsewhere the provider's hosting model does. About the two providers the public record supports four kinds of statement and no more: Stripe runs on Amazon Web Services and names no AWS region; Adyen runs its own data centers, names five integration regions and lists its sites by continent or country, no finer; Stripe says it stores Indian payment system data only in India and lists the features that cost, while Adyen describes an isolated India environment; and Adyen says it accepts payments in several data centers at once and that its load balancers fail over between them. Neither says between which places takeover happens or how fast, and Stripe has described takeover only for one system, a two-region design for billing usage events (2025).
thesis.disputed_by: The view that multi-region operation is an engineering choice made for latency and uptime, that any provider of this size must be active-active across regions, and that its layout can be worked out from its cloud provider or its customer list.
thesis.so_what: The reader answers 'where is our members' data' with two differently shaped facts (a cloud provider whose regions are not named, and a list of regions and countries with no cities and no commitment that data stays there), puts residency and failover questions to each provider in writing, and expects a localization rule to change product behavior, not only storage.
thesis.how_why: The Reserve Bank of India's 2018 circular requires that payment system data be stored 'only in India' and gives supervisory access, not privacy, as the reason; its 2019 clarification allows processing abroad if the data is brought back within 24 hours. Stripe's page on the move (last updated 2023) lists the cost: payment information 'can no longer be cloned into or out of India', and one card can have two fingerprints. The EU's operational-resilience regulation, applied from 17 January 2025, says in terms that it imposes no localization duty. On hosting the difference is documented: Stripe on AWS (2023 press release, 2024, current documentation), Adyen 'in several data centers around the world' (2021) for reasons it called 'part historical, part legal, and part technical', confirmed in 2025 and 2026; Adyen's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) names five regions an integrator can address: Europe, the United States, Australia, Northeast Asia and India. Its website (n.d., accessed November 2026) lists data centers in Europe, the United States, India, Singapore, Japan and Australia and says payments are 'stored in Europe and our isolated India environment', and its peak-season documentation calls the architecture 'active/active' and says load balancers 'manage the failover to the other data centers'. Stripe's Privacy Center (n.d., accessed November 2026) says payment system data is stored only on servers in India where the rule requires it. Nothing first-party names an AWS region Stripe runs in, a city for an Adyen data center, or the topology or timing of a failover at either company, or any mechanism beyond Adyen's load-balancer sentence, and Stripe has published no statement on takeover for payments, only a two-region design with failover for billing usage events (2025). The public record stops there, and so does the chapter.

supporting_claims.claim: Two forces spread a payment platform across regions, distance and law, and where a localization law applies it fixes where data is stored before any latency or availability goal is considered.

A localization law is a product constraint as much as a storage one: in the best-documented case, India, Stripe moved the servers that store India data into the country, stopped payment details crossing the border, gave one card two fingerprints and switched features off.

Where no such law applies the provider's hosting model decides, and that much is documented: Stripe runs on Amazon Web Services and names no AWS region; Adyen runs its own infrastructure, names five integration regions, and lists its data centers on its website by continent or country (Europe, the United States, India, Singapore, Japan, Australia), no finer.

Neither company has published how takeover between its sites works. Adyen documents an 'active/active, stateless architecture' whose load balancers 'manage the failover to the other data centers', and says payments are stored in Europe and an isolated India environment, but gives no topology, timings or mechanism; Stripe says nothing on serving from several regions or on failover; the public record stops there.

An integrator therefore answers 'where is our customers' payment data' with two differently shaped documented facts and a list of questions put to each provider in writing, never with an inferred topology.

role.contribution: Adds the constraint that comes from outside engineering (law and hosting) and draws the boundary of the public record on regions and failover, so that no later page describes a topology neither company has published.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene to in-practice: the questionnaire is posed in the first section and answered in the sixth

flow.rationale: The reader meets a question that invites an inferred answer, then gets the vocabulary to read sources (two pulls, residency against localization, three placements). The law case comes before the hosting case because the thesis says law decides first, and because India is the one placement with a documented cost; hosting then covers everywhere else. The comparison needs both. Larkfield's answer needs the comparison; the failure section needs the answer to contrast with; the list of where the evidence stops comes last in the body because each item on it is only meaningful once the reader has seen what is documented next to it. Putting the list first would read as a disclaimer; putting hosting before India would present the provider's choice as the general rule and the law as an exception, which is the view the thesis disputes.

hook.content: A colleague writes in a design document: 'Stripe runs active-active in three AWS regions, so our European members' data never leaves the EU.' The sentence reads like knowledge. As of November 2026 the public record supports one word of it: AWS.

bridge.from_reader_world: An engineer is used to reading a system's regions off its documentation or its cloud console, and to choosing them for latency and uptime.
bridge.to_topic: A payment provider's regions are chosen partly by law, and neither Stripe nor Adyen publishes its layout, so the engineer's habit of inferring a topology produces sentences nobody can source.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The previous chapter's data was divided by engineers and described at length by both companies, while this chapter's is divided by law in a part of the record where little is published, which is why a confident sentence about a provider's regions can be almost entirely unsupported. Active-active is glossed where the design-document sentence first uses it (several regions serving at once).

evidence.what: The design-document sentence 'Stripe runs active-active in three AWS regions, so our European members' data never leaves the EU'; of its claims only AWS is documented (Stripe newsroom, 23 January 2023).
evidence.shows: The gap between how such a sentence sounds and what can be sourced is the chapter's problem.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Law settles where payment data is stored where a localization rule applies, the provider's hosting model settles it elsewhere, and the public record supports four kinds of statement about Stripe and Adyen, which the chapter takes in turn (hosting for each, the regions Adyen names, what each has said about India, Adyen's statement that it serves from several data centers at once and fails over between them); neither describes how takeover (one site taking over another's traffic) works, between which places or how fast.

transition_in.introduces: What can be said instead: the thesis and its four documented statements.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: One Question, Two Providers
sections.controlling_idea: A studio chain that uses both providers asks Larkfield where its members' payment data is stored, and the first draft of the answer is an inferred topology.

advances_thesis.how: Poses the integrator's question with a studio whose data sits at both providers, and shows the inferred answer the chapter replaces.

transition_in.introduces: A real-looking question that needs a sourced answer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In April 2027 a pilates chain in Hamburg, one of the 1,140 studios that take online payments on Stripe and front-desk payments on Adyen, sends Larkfield a questionnaire asking where its members' payment data is stored and whether it leaves the European Union.

evidence.what: 1,140 studios onboarded before 2024 in NL and DE are on Stripe online and Adyen terminals; Jonas Weber owns compliance; Femke de Graaf leads payments engineering. The questionnaire is a new ledger addition.
evidence.shows: A studio on both providers makes the question need two answers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Tom Hendriks's first draft says both providers keep the data in EU regions and fail over inside the EU, and Femke de Graaf returns it asking for the source of each clause; he finds a source for half a clause (Adyen's website says the payments it processes are stored in Europe, which is not the EU) and none for the rest.

evidence.what: Tom Hendriks built the payment service in 2024; the draft answer is illustration.
evidence.shows: The inferred answer is the natural one for an engineer, which is why the chapter is needed.

evidence.what: Adyen infrastructure page (n.d., accessed 2026-11): 'All payments processed are stored in Europe and our isolated India environment.' (https://www.adyen.com/infrastructure).
evidence.shows: The one clause of the draft that has a published source, and why it still does not support 'EU regions'.

transition_in.introduces: The draft answer and the demand for sources, which the rest of the chapter meets.

sections.heading: Two Pulls Toward Regions: Distance and Law
sections.controlling_idea: Distance and law both push a payment platform into regions, law wins where it applies, and the three ways of placing data cost a money path different things.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the two causes, the vocabulary (residency, localization, active-active, active-passive) and the trade-offs, so the documented cases can be read.

flow.rationale: The engineering pull first because the reader knows it; then the legal pull and its vocabulary; then the designs that answer both; then their costs side by side.

transition_in.introduces: The vocabulary needed to read the sources: why platforms spread, and what the placements are called.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Checking Tom's clauses needs the sources' vocabulary; distance is the engineering pull: a payment waits on every network hop, so a platform puts the systems that answer close to where payments start.

evidence.what: Adyen, 'Building a GlobalStream' (page dated 6 October 2025): 'data must remain close to producers to reduce latency and meet regulations, while also being centralized for analytics', with the example of a payment on a beach in Australia that should not be 'sent to Europe' (https://www.adyen.com/knowledge-hub/building-a-global-stream).
evidence.shows: A first-party statement of both pulls in one sentence, with latency as the first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Law is the other pull, and it comes in two strengths that are often confused: data residency is the fact of where data is stored, data localization is a law that requires it, and the European rules a Dutch platform meets regulate transfers and resilience without requiring storage in the Union.

evidence.what: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (DORA), recital 82, applying from 17 January 2025: 'This Regulation does not impose a data localisation obligation as it does not require data storage or processing to be undertaken in the Union.' (http://publications.europa.eu/resource/celex/32022R2554.ENG).
evidence.shows: The EU's resilience law for financial entities says in terms that it is not a localization law.

evidence.what: Stripe DPA FAQ (n.d., accessed 2026-11): 'Under Article 46 GDPR, the SCCs are one of the ways that organizations can transfer personal data to certain countries, outside of the European Economic Area, including the United States.' (https://stripe.com/us/legal/dpa/faqs).
evidence.shows: European privacy law conditions transfers; it does not forbid them.

transition_in.introduces: The pull they do not, and the two words for it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Once data sits in several regions, a platform must choose between active-passive, where one region serves and another waits, and active-active, where several serve at once, and on a money path the second choice raises the question of which region may write a given balance.

evidence.what: Uber Engineering, 5 December 2018: its payments platform's 'primary design goals were high reliability through an active-active architecture, exactly-once payment processing by the means of idempotency and strong consistency' (https://www.uber.com/blog/payments-platform/); evidence age 8 years.
evidence.shows: Some payment systems publish this choice; it shows what a published statement looks like, against which Stripe's and Adyen's silence is measured.

evidence.what: Chapter 38's consistency boundary and chapter 37's unknown outcome: two regions writing the same record need an order between their writes; a takeover leaves in-flight payments unknown.
evidence.shows: Why the choice is harder for money than for a stateless service.

transition_in.carries_over: Why data ends up in several regions.
transition_in.introduces: How the regions share the work.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three placements exist (one writer with a standby, several writers, and a partition by country), and each buys something different at a different cost to the record of money; before the table the unit says what its last column shows, with the provider evidence the later section sets out: the only placement with a full provider case is the one a law forced (India), Adyen's documentation calls its architecture active/active with failover between data centers, Stripe describes two regions at once only for billing usage events, and neither company says which site writes which record.

evidence.what: Rows: active-passive; active-active; partitioned by jurisdiction. Columns: what it buys; what it costs on a money path; what is documented for Stripe and Adyen (active-passive: not stated by either; active-active: not found for Stripe's payments (a two-region design is published for billing usage events, 2025), and for Adyen the 'active/active' statement of its peak season readiness documentation, with the write rule 'Not public'; the third: Stripe's India move, page updated 2023, and Adyen's 'isolated India environment', n.d.).
evidence.shows: The trade-off table: the only placement with a documented provider case is the one a law forced.
evidence.source: author's analysis; Stripe India page, last updated 16 May 2023; Adyen infrastructure page and peak season readiness documentation, n.d., accessed 2026-11

evidence.what: Placeholder 39-three-placements: three panels showing a standby, two writers and a walled-off country.
evidence.shows: Makes the three placements visible.

transition_in.introduces: A third placement and the costs of all three.

sections.heading: When a Law Decides: India's Storage Rule
sections.controlling_idea: India's rule shows a localization law deciding storage for supervisory reasons, and Stripe's page on its response shows the cost falling on product features and identifiers.

advances_thesis.how: The one localization case with a first-party account from one of the two companies: the rule's text, then what moving cost.

flow.rationale: The 2018 rule and its 2019 clarification, then Stripe's 2021 to 2023 response, then what the response means. Adyen's India account (p28) follows Stripe's, so the two providers' India costs sit together.

transition_in.introduces: The documented case of it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Reserve Bank of India's 2018 circular requires payment system data to be stored only in India, gives supervisory access as the reason, and was clarified in 2019 to allow processing abroad if the data returns within 24 hours.

evidence.what: RBI circular RBI/2017-18/153, 6 April 2018: 'All system providers shall ensure that the entire data relating to payment systems operated by them are stored in a system only in India'; 'it is important to have unfettered supervisory access to data'; compliance to be reported 'latest by October 15, 2018' (https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/NotificationUser.aspx?Id=11244&Mode=0). Evidence age 8 years.
evidence.shows: The rule's text and its stated reason, which is supervision and not privacy.

evidence.what: RBI FAQ, 26 June 2019: 'There is no bar on processing of payment transactions outside India'; data 'should be deleted from the systems abroad and brought back to India not later than the one business day or 24 hours from payment processing, whichever is earlier'; applies to 'payment gateways, third party vendors and other entities' (https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/FAQView.aspx?Id=130). Evidence age 7 years.
evidence.shows: Storage is fixed, processing is not, and the rule reaches providers, not only banks.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stripe's page on its response, last updated in May 2023, records that it was moving the servers that store India data into the country and that the move stopped payment details crossing the border, split the card fingerprint and switched several features off; two current Stripe pages state that the data is stored on servers in India. The card fingerprint is glossed at first use (an identifier that lets a merchant recognize the same card number across customers without seeing it), and so are connected accounts (the businesses on a platform).

evidence.what: Stripe, 'Important updates on Stripe data storage migration in India', last updated 16 May 2023: 'we're moving the servers that store India data to be located within the country'; 'a substantive infrastructure change'; 'Payment information can no longer be cloned into or out of India'; 'the same card details can have two different fingerprints, one for India and another for the rest of the world'; Card Updater, Revenue Recognition and Sigma 'temporarily disabled in India' from 30 April 2021 (https://stripe.com/india-data-storage-faq). Evidence age 3.5 years.
evidence.shows: The documented product cost of localization, in Stripe's own list.

evidence.what: Stripe Privacy Center (n.d., accessed 2026-11): 'Where required payment system data will be stored only on servers in India in accordance with the RBI data localization requirements.' (https://stripe.com/us/legal/privacy-center). Stripe Service Providers list (last updated 27 September 2026): 'Stripe India Private Limited stores certain data on servers located in India' (https://stripe.com/us/legal/service-providers).
evidence.shows: Current confirmation that the localization still holds.

transition_in.introduces: What complying with it cost one provider.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The fingerprint is the telling line: an identifier that was global becomes two, so whatever relied on matching it (duplicate checks, saved cards, fraud signals) stops matching across the border, which makes a localization rule a product constraint.

evidence.what: Stripe documents the two fingerprints and the end of cloning; that fraud and duplicate checks keyed on the fingerprint stop matching across the border is the author's inference and goes in an INFERENCE block.
evidence.shows: Generalizes the case to what any merchant should expect from a new localization rule (AC-2).
evidence.source: author's inference from the Stripe page

evidence.what: Placeholder 39-one-card-two-fingerprints: one card, a border, two different identifiers.
evidence.shows: Makes the broken global identifier memorable.

transition_in.introduces: Why one line of it matters most.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adyen documents a smaller cost of the same kind: India needs a separate company account, and velocity risk rules start there without the transaction history they rely on.

evidence.what: Adyen India compliance guide (n.d., accessed 2026-11): local processing needs 'a separate company account for your business in India'. India go-live checklist (n.d., accessed 2026-11): velocity risk rules 'will not work as well for your India company account at first, because they rely on historical transaction data'.
evidence.shows: The second provider's documented product cost of the same partition.

transition_in.carries_over: A localization rule as a product constraint, shown by Stripe's fingerprint.
transition_in.introduces: Adyen's documented cost of its India account.

sections.heading: What Each Company Has Published About Where It Runs
sections.controlling_idea: Outside a localization law the hosting model decides where data sits; the two companies have documented opposite hosting models, Adyen also a list of data-center regions, a storage sentence and the statement that it fails over between data centers, and neither how takeover works.

advances_thesis.how: Lays out the dated first-party statements on hosting and regions for each company.

flow.rationale: Stripe's hosting, then Adyen's, then the regions Adyen lets an integrator address, which have no Stripe counterpart.

transition_in.carries_over: A country where the law decides.
transition_in.introduces: Everywhere else, where the provider's hosting does.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stripe has said since 2023 that it runs on Amazon Web Services and has confirmed it since, but names no AWS region, says nothing on how regions share or take over work for payments (its one published two-region design, of January 2025, is for billing usage events), names only two countries (the United States and India) and only for login and identity data, and tells its users that personal data may be processed in any country where it does business.

evidence.what: Stripe newsroom, 23 January 2023: 'Stripe has long relied on AWS to provide the core compute infrastructure on which Stripe is built'; David Singleton: 'We couldn't run without AWS—and we wouldn't want to' (https://stripe.com/us/newsroom/news/amazon-and-stripe). Evidence age nearly 4 years.
evidence.shows: The hosting statement.

evidence.what: AWS Cloud Operations blog with Stripe co-authors, 24 October 2024: 'a sophisticated microservice environment built on top of AWS'. Stripe security documentation (n.d., accessed 2026-11): the card data vault runs 'in an isolated Amazon Web Services (AWS) environment that's separate from the rest of the Stripe infrastructure' (https://docs.stripe.com/security).
evidence.shows: Newer sources confirm the 2023 statement.

evidence.what: Stripe Privacy Center (n.d., accessed 2026-11): 'As a global business, Personal Data may be transferred to, and processed, in any country where we do business'; 'including to the United States'. API reference: base URL https://api.stripe.com.
evidence.shows: No residency promise and no region an integrator can choose.

evidence.what: Stripe Privacy Center (n.d., accessed 2026-11), 'Why is Stripe storing authentication and authorization data globally?': 'a robust, multi-region infrastructure dedicated to optimizing authentication, authorization, and identity management. This infrastructure spans multiple geographic regions, specifically including our data centers located in the United States and India'; 'this global storage strategy does not extend to any transactional information or other data related to End Customers'.
evidence.shows: The only places Stripe names are two countries, for login and identity data, not for payment data.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adyen has said since 2021 that it runs its own infrastructure in data centers and not in a public cloud, its 2025 and 2026 statements confirm it and show the estate growing, its corporate website lists the data centers by continent or country and says where processed payments are stored, and its documentation states an active/active architecture with failover between data centers, without topology, timings or mechanism. For Mila's EUR 120.00 at Studio Noord, the website's continent-level sentence is the whole public answer.

evidence.what: Adyen, 'Design to Duty', 28 July 2021: 'We manage our own infrastructure in several data centers around the world'; 'The reasons we are not deploying to the cloud are part historical, part legal, and part technical' (https://www.adyen.com/knowledge-hub/design-to-duty-adyen-architecture). Evidence age 5 years.
evidence.shows: The hosting statement and its stated reasons.

evidence.what: Adyen, 31 October 2025: 'end-to-end ownership over every layer, from our data centers to our application logic'; Adyen, August 2026: 'tens of thousands of hosts spread across tens of data centres'; H1 2026 results, 13 August 2026: 'The majority of our CapEx is invested in data centers'.
evidence.shows: Confirmation in 2025 and 2026, and an order of magnitude without locations.

evidence.what: Adyen infrastructure page (n.d., accessed 2026-11; https://www.adyen.com/infrastructure): 'Adyen currently hosts its main systems in separate data centers in Europe, the United States, India, Singapore, Japan and Australia'; 'All payments processed are stored in Europe and our isolated India environment'; 'a redundant and stateless service-oriented architecture (SOA) that simultaneously accepts payments on multiple physical hosting locations'. The Dutch and Portuguese versions of the page list fewer places (Europe, the United States and Australia; two data centers in Europe and two in the United States).
evidence.shows: Adyen names places at the level of a continent or a country, states where payments are stored and says it accepts payments in several locations at once; the page is undated and its translations disagree, so it is read as a summary, not a commitment.

evidence.what: Adyen documentation, 'Peak season readiness' (n.d., accessed 2026-11; https://docs.adyen.com/industries/peak-season): 'Our active/active, stateless architecture allows us to distribute transactions across a pool of highly available resources'; 'With load balancers in front of every data center, transactions can be equally processed through any available data center. In the event that a data center is unavailable, these load balancers also manage the failover to the other data centers.'
evidence.shows: Adyen states that it serves from several data centers and fails over between them; it does not say between which, how fast, or what happens to the systems that hold state (ruling 45).

transition_in.introduces: Owned infrastructure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adyen's documentation names five regions an integrator can address for online payments, assigns each country's terminals to a data center region, and says a company account's data centers (and prefixes, the account's own start of its live endpoint addresses) are visible in its Customer Area; what it has published about rerouting names no destination, and its privacy statement allows disclosure outside the EEA.

evidence.what: Adyen docs (n.d., accessed 2026-11), best practices for web integrations: 'Europe (EU) live', 'United States (US) live', 'Australia (AU) live', 'Northeast Asia (NEA) live', 'India (IN) live'. Live endpoints: 'you can see the configured data centres and prefixes for your company account'; 'If you need to connect to a certain data center of the Adyen payments platform (for example, US or AU data centers), you can set up location-based live endpoints'; 'alternative routing can be enabled to backup infrastructure and new infrastructure can be provisioned on demand'. Building a cloud integration: a 'Regional data center overview' table assigns each country to a data center region (the Netherlands and Germany to EU); 'make sure to select the data center closest to your geographical location'.
evidence.shows: Regions are part of Adyen's integration surface; locations and takeover are not described.

evidence.what: Adyen privacy statement (version of 4 August 2025; https://www.adyen.com/privacy-policy): information 'may be disclosed to other Adyen group companies outside of the European Economic Area'.
evidence.shows: The storage sentence on Adyen's website is not a residency promise.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong: The Sentence Nobody Can Source
sections.controlling_idea: The failure this chapter guards against is a commitment built on an inferred topology, found by asking each clause for its source and repaired by a written answer from the provider.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the cost of ignoring the boundary of the record: detection and recovery for the chapter's own failure mode.

transition_in.introduces: What happens when the unsourced one is sent instead.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An inferred topology, The Borrowed Blueprint in one sentence, fails late: it enters a customer contract or a recovery plan as fact, and is discovered to be a guess when an auditor asks for evidence or a regional outage behaves differently from the plan; the one failover Larkfield can rehearse is its own K8 switch, its answer to The Single Rail, made more valuable, by the author's judgement, because the providers' hosting differs.

evidence.what: Tom's draft sentence, had it been sent; K8's switch between providers is Larkfield's documented failover, and that the two providers' hosting differs (AWS; own data centers) is documented, while their independence under failure is the author's judgement.
evidence.shows: Detection is a source per clause; recovery is the provider's written answer; the one thing Larkfield can rehearse is its own switch.

sections.heading: Where the Evidence Stops
sections.controlling_idea: Seven things about the two providers' regions and failover are not in any first-party source found as of November 2026, and each is a question to ask, not a gap to fill by inference.

advances_thesis.how: States the boundary of the public record item by item (AC-3).

transition_in.introduces: The exact list of what would have to be inferred.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Not public for Stripe: AWS region names and count, whether the API is served from several regions at once, and where European payment data is stored or any commitment to keep it in Europe; not public for Adyen: data-center cities and operators, whether 'stored in Europe' is a commitment and what it covers, and what its isolated India environment changes in features; not public for either: how takeover works (Adyen states that its load balancers fail over between data centers, not between which, how fast or with what effect on records being written).

evidence.what: Searches on 17 November 2026 of both documentation indexes and sitemaps (docs.stripe.com, docs.adyen.com), both help-center sitemaps (support.stripe.com, help.adyen.com), both engineering blogs (stripe.dev/blog, adyen.com/knowledge-hub), both companies' legal and privacy pages, Adyen's corporate and investor pages and the web found no first-party statement on any of the seven items.
evidence.shows: Absence of a statement, recorded as such.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The chapter's two halves say the same thing from opposite sides: where a law speaks, the placement of data is known and even its product cost is documented; where no law speaks, placement is whatever the provider's hosting makes it, and Stripe says almost nothing while Adyen offers a few undated sentences on its website and in its documentation. So the better-documented topology is the one a regulator forced into the open.
conclusion.so_what: The reader stops treating a provider's regions as something to work out and treats them as something to ask for: two documented facts of different shape, a written question for each gap, and an expectation that the next localization rule will change identifiers and features, not only disks.

callback.to: The design-document sentence of the opening: 'Stripe runs active-active in three AWS regions, so our European members' data never leaves the EU.'

takeaway.content: For each provider, write one page with two columns, 'documented, with source and date' and 'asked in writing, with the answer', and let no sentence about regions or failover into a contract or a recovery plan unless it sits in one of them.

open_questions: Stripe's India page describes Card Updater, Revenue Recognition and Sigma as 'temporarily disabled' and was last updated on 16 May 2023; whether they were restored is not stated on it. The article says so.

Adyen's infrastructure page is undated and its Dutch and Portuguese versions list fewer data-center regions and no India environment; the article cites the English page and says so. Whether to rely on it at all is the author's call.
